extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of social theory, anthropology, and comparative history
extracted.subtask_description: An explanatory account of the general law that systems (biological, social, linguistic, artistic, musical, economic) evolve from relative homogeneity to increasing heterogeneity, illustrated across anatomy, society, language, arts, and industry. Intended as a comprehensive, comparative exposition of that single evolutionary principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law: change from the homogeneous to the heterogeneous
rubrics_metrics.description: The central principle that organisms, societies, languages, arts, industries, and other products of human thought and action advance by a process of differentiation — i.e. from a relatively homogeneous state toward increasing heterogeneity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as a general law illustrated repeatedly: in individual development (embryology), in racial differences, in social organization, in language, in the arts, and in industry. The text repeatedly returns to this formula and uses it as the organizing explanatory criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anatomical indicator of heterogeneity (brain/jaw proportions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Civilized humans exhibit relatively larger cranial bones and relatively smaller jaw bones, implying a more complex or heterogeneous nervous system compared with 'savage' races.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author cites nursery observations (infant European features resembling 'lower human races' that later differentiate) and ratios of cerebrum to subjacent ganglia as evidence that individual development continues the change from homogeneous to heterogeneous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase of racial heterogeneity over time
rubrics_metrics.description: Mankind, as a whole, has become more heterogeneous — evidenced by ethnological divisions and the emergence of new varieties within a few generations (e.g., Anglo-Americans).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even allowing multiple origins of humanity, continuous divergence within each stock produces many widely different tribes; philological evidence and recent examples (America, Australia) support rising heterogeneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social differentiation into governing and governed
rubrics_metrics.description: Primitive societies are relatively homogeneous; social evolution shows incipient differentiation where authority emerges (chieftainship) and gradually becomes a distinct governing class with different occupations and lifestyle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early rulers initially performed the same tasks as others; with progress, rulership becomes hereditary, rulers cease manual provision and 'assume the sole office of ruling'. This is a primary axis of social heterogeneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co‑ordinate differentiation of civil, religious, and ceremonial authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: As societies evolve, government diversifies into civil power, religion (priesthood), and manners/ceremonial usages, each becoming distinct controlling agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: earliest rulers regarded as divine; king as chief priest; titles of honour deriving from divine names; religious law containing civil regulation; and the slow divergence into separate Church/State/ceremonial institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increasing complexity of political and religious organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Advanced nations show elaborate, multi-tiered political and religious structures (monarch, ministers, lords, commons, courts, revenue offices; archbishops to sextons; colleges; sects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text enumerates administrative departments, provincial and municipal governments, ecclesiastical hierarchies, and multiplying independent sects as markers of heterogeneity in institutional arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Segregation into classes and division of labor
rubrics_metrics.description: Societies evolve from members performing the same tasks to minute division of labour among distinct classes and orders of workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations include caste divisions, incorporated guilds, and the transformation of solitary producers into specialized producers working under masters; this minute division is a key index of social heterogeneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic and national economic specialization
rubrics_metrics.description: With improved transport and trade, different districts and nations specialize in particular industries, increasing heterogeneity across localities and between peoples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: calico manufacture in one county, woollens in another, silks elsewhere; free-trade will intensify specialization across nations — leading to mutual dependence and heterogeneity of functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language evolution: multiplication of parts of speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Language progresses from simpler systems (exclamations, nouns+verbs) to differentiated parts of speech (active/usive verbs, abstract/concrete nouns, moods, tenses, persons, numbers, cases, auxiliaries, adjectives, adverbs, pronouns, prepositions, articles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This subdivision of functions is cited as the reason English is 'superior', and is used to illustrate how increased functional differentiation equates to linguistic heterogeneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lexical differentiation: divergence of allied word‑meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: Words originally applied broadly become modified into families of distinct terms expressing smaller and smaller distinctions, producing a large heterogeneous vocabulary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philological evidence of root families diverging into many modified forms is used; morphology (derivatives, compound terms) furthers differentiation until thousands of unlike words represent many unlike objects/actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplication and divergence of languages (language families)
rubrics_metrics.description: Languages and language families become distinct through continuous divergence as peoples diffuse geographically; dialectical variation within nations is further evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Indo-European family, possible single or multiple stocks, and the same diffusion process producing racial differentiation as producing linguistic differentiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolution of written language: pictorial to phonetic to alphabet to printing
rubrics_metrics.description: Written forms grow from mural/pictorial representations to picture-writing (ideographic), to hieroglyphic families (kuriological/imitative and tropical/symbolic), to hieratic/epistolographic forms, then to phonetic symbols and alphabets, and finally to printing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Egyptian and Mexican examples: mural decoration tied to religion/government, simplification of pictured figures into symbols, occasional phonetic use leading toward alphabetic systems, and later printing multiplying written forms for distinct purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiation of arts (painting and sculpture from architecture/religion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Painting and sculpture originate as appendages of architecture and religion and gradually separate into independent arts with increasingly heterogeneous subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Egyptian and Assyrian mural art tied to temples/palaces and governmental/religious functions; over time these arts separate from architecture/religion (Greek, Christian examples) and then diversify into many genres (historical, landscape, genre, still-life, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural heterogeneity of artworks (perspective, light, colour, composition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Early works exhibit uniformity (single plane, uniform light, primary colours, repeated motifs); modern artworks display varied distances, contrasts in light, intermediate tints, asymmetry and varied compositions, indicating higher heterogeneity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparisons: Egyptian fresco/statue (one plane, uniform light, primary colours, repeated motifs) vs advanced Greek/modern works (varied distances, shades, asymmetry) as measures of increase in heterogeneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation and differentiation of rhythmical arts (poetry, music, dancing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Originally united rhythmic expressions (speech, sound, motion) in religious festivals differentiate into distinct arts: poetry, music, and dance, each assuming separate forms and social functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence from barbarous tribes and ancient records: dances with monotonous chant and percussion in ceremonies; Greek and Hebrew examples of chant, dance, and song in worship; gradual emergence of secular forms and distinct poetic/musical roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical differentiation: instruments, modes, melody, and complex rhythm
rubrics_metrics.description: Music evolves from percussive, repetitive forms (time-marking) toward melodic complexity via more-stringed instruments, multiple modes (Dorian, Ionian, Phrygian, Lydian), and ultimately complex rhythm separated from speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Progression: percussive instruments → Egyptian 3-string lyre → Greek tetrachord → lyres with 7–8 strings → double octave systems and multiple modes; separation of music from poetry allowed greater melodic and rhythmic heterogeneity.
